title: Perfect tensor quotient coaugmentation and its completion diagrams
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$, where complete means that $R\to\varprojlim_{j\geq1}R/(\pi^j)$ is an isomorphism. Put $A_j=R/(\pi^j)$. Let $P,Q$ be bounded cochain complexes of finitely generated projective $R$-modules, representing perfect objects of $D(R)$ [def-pc-perfect-ring-complex, def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. With signed total tensor [def-pc-tensor-complex-sheaves] put $V=\operatorname{Tot}(P\otimes_RQ)$ and
$$ U_j=(P\otimes_RA_j)\otimes_{A_j}(Q\otimes_RA_j). $$
Totalization is understood in this formula. Use the strict quotient transitions and the functorial shifted-cone model $H(U)=\operatorname{Cone}(1-t:\prod_jU_j\to\prod_jU_j)[-1]$ [lem-weil-pbc-ringed-strict-tower-homotopy-limit], applied to the one-point ringed site. Order its degree-$q$ coordinates as $(x,y)\in(\prod_jU_j)^q\oplus(\prod_jU_j)^{q-1}$, with differential $d(x,y)=(dx,(1-t)x-dy)$. Let $e_{P,Q}:V\to H(U)$ be the chain map whose first product coordinate sends $x\otimes y$ to $((x\bmod\pi^j)\otimes(y\bmod\pi^j))_j$ and whose shifted-product coordinate is zero.
Then $V$ is bounded finite projective, $U_j$ is canonically $V\otimes_RA_j$ by $(x\otimes a)\otimes(y\otimes b)\mapsto(x\otimes y)\otimes ab$, and $e_{P,Q}$ is a quasi-isomorphism. More precisely, the quotient tower is termwise surjective, its termwise inverse limit is $V$ with these quotient projections, and $1-t$ is degreewise surjective with that kernel. In $D(R)$ this is the canonical completion isomorphism of the ordinary derived module tensor, natural in the two perfect objects and independent of bounded projective models.
Its quotient-coordinate formula intertwines the associator for three perfect complexes, the degree-$(i,j)$ Koszul symmetry, both multiplication unitors and the coefficient unit. It is compatible with every further quotient $A_m\to A_n$ for $m\geq n\geq1$. For a continuous local finite free homomorphism of complete discrete valuation rings $R\to S$, it is also compatible with extension of $P,Q$ to $S$, the balanced scalar tensorator, and the canonical completion comparisons. Here the $\pi$-power filtration on $S$ and the uniformizer-power filtration on $S$ are compared by their cofinal quotient maps; the assertion concerns the induced derived completion maps. The identity and iterated-extension squares commute, with the same quotient and zero shifted coordinates.

proof.text: For a finitely generated projective module $M$, choose a surjection $p:R^a\to M$ using finite generators and split it by projectivity, obtaining $i:M\to R^a$ with $pi=1$. Tensoring two such splittings makes $P^r\otimes_RQ^s$ a retract of $R^{a_rb_s}$. A finite direct sum of these retractions makes $V^q$ finite projective. If $P,Q$ have supports in $[a,b],[c,d]$, $V$ has support in $[a+c,b+d]$. This proves the asserted bounded finite projectivity without any choice of compatible bases.

proof.text: The balanced map $\phi_j:(P\otimes_RA_j)\otimes_{A_j}(Q\otimes_RA_j)\to V\otimes_RA_j$ sends $(x\otimes a)\otimes(y\otimes b)$ to $(x\otimes y)\otimes ab$. Its inverse sends $(x\otimes y)\otimes c$ to $(x\otimes1)\otimes(y\otimes c)$. Both are balanced, and their composites are identities on pure tensors, hence on every element. On the summand of bidegree $(r,s)$ both differentials are $d_P\otimes1+(-1)^r1\otimes d_Q$, so these are cochain isomorphisms. Reducing $ab$ to a smaller quotient is the product of the reductions. Thus the isomorphisms identify every transition with the ordinary quotient transition of $V$. Here $M\otimes_RA_j\cong M/\pi^jM$ sends $m\otimes\bar r$ to the class of $rm$, with inverse $[m]\mapsto m\otimes1$; the balancing relations check both composites.

For each $M=V^q$, use the finite splitting $M\xrightarrow{i}R^a\xrightarrow{p}M$ of step 1 and put $E=ip$. A compatible family in $M/\pi^jM$ embeds, by the reduced maps $i_j$, in $\varprojlim_j A_j^a=R^a$, where the equality follows coordinate by coordinate from the assumed completeness of $R$. Its image $z$ satisfies $Ez=z$, since this holds in every quotient and $R^a\to\varprojlim A_j^a$ is injective. Hence $z=i(pz)$ and the family is the reduction of $pz$. Injectivity follows from that same embedding. The inverse is linear, and this identification commutes with every module map because its quotient coordinates do. Applied degreewise, it identifies the termwise limit complex with $V$ and its projections with the given quotient maps. Each transition is surjective: $M/\pi^{j+1}M\to M/\pi^jM$ sends any lift of a class to that class.

proof.text: Write $B=\prod_jU_j$ and $f=1-t$. In degree $q$, for any $b=(b_j)$ choose $a_1=0$ and recursively choose $a_{j+1}$ lifting $a_j-b_j$ along the surjective transition. Then $f(a)=b$. Also $f(a)=0$ means exactly that $(a_j)$ is compatible. By step 3, its kernel is the quotient image $c(V^q)$, and $c$ is injective. The quotient maps are cochain maps and $fc=0$, so $v\mapsto(c(v),0)$ is a cochain map into $H(U)$ with precisely the coordinates specified for $e_{P,Q}$.

The surjective-module-complex-tower theorem applies to $A_j$, whose limit is $R$ by hypothesis, and to $U_j\cong V\otimes_RA_j$: its transitions are scalar-linear and surjective in each degree by steps 2--3. It gives the derived-limit Roos triangle. To fix the actual quasi-isomorphism, let $(x,y)$ be a degree-$q$ cycle of our fibre model. Then $dx=0$ and $fx=dy$. Choose $a\in B^{q-1}$ with $fa=y$ by step 4. Subtract $d(a,0)=(da,fa)$; the cycle becomes $(x-da,0)$ with $f(x-da)=0$, hence is $(c(v),0)$ for a unique cycle $v\in V^q$. If $(c(v),0)=d(a,b)$, then $c(v)=da$ and $fa=db$. Choose $z\in B^{q-2}$ with $fz=b$. Now $f(a-dz)=0$, so $a-dz=c(w)$ and $c(v)=c(dw)$; injectivity of $c$ gives $v=dw$. This proves surjectivity and injectivity on cohomology for the specified $e_{P,Q}$.

Projective modules are flat, and bounded-above complexes of flat modules are K-flat; this applies to $P,Q,V$ and, after base change, to their quotient complexes, since the splittings of step 1 remain split after tensoring. Thus the derived monoidal computation identifies $V$ with $P\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}Q$. The K-flat scalar-tower realization, for the one-point site and $R\to A_j$, identifies the actual derived reduction unit with $v\mapsto v\otimes1$ and the derived adjoint transition with the strict quotient map. Countable products of modules are exact (choose preimages coordinatewise), and the small-module-diagram theorem, with the one-point site and either terminal index category or $\mathbf N_{\geq1}^{\mathrm{op}}$, gives the Grothendieck hypotheses for modules and towers, so the exact-products Roos comparison identifies localization of the zero-second-coordinate kernel map with the canonical derived-limit augmentation. Consequently our quasi-isomorphism is the canonical completion map of this derived tensor, not merely an isomorphism between its source and target. The free-module functor on underlying sets, with its evaluation surjection, supplies the functorial flat resolutions required by the derived-monoidal theorem.

For cochain maps $a:P\to P'$, $b:Q\to Q'$, reduction of $a(x)\otimes b(y)$ equals $(a\bmod\pi^j)(\bar x)\otimes(b\bmod\pi^j)(\bar y)$, giving a strictly commuting augmentation square. Bounded-above projective complexes are K-projective, and the K-projective Hom bijection says that every derived morphism between our bounded projective models is represented by a cochain map uniquely up to homotopy. These squares therefore give naturality for all derived morphisms: tensoring a homotopy in the first variable gives $h\otimes1$; in the second variable it gives $x\otimes y\mapsto(-1)^{\deg x}x\otimes h(y)$. A strict tower homotopy $h_j$ induces the fibre homotopy $(x,y)\mapsto((h_jx_j)_j,-(h_jy_j)_j)$; substituting into $dH+Hd$ gives the difference of the induced fibre maps. Thus both the tensor and fibre maps depend only on the homotopy classes. An isomorphism of derived models is represented by maps inverse up to homotopy, so the comparison is an isomorphism and the strictly commuting squares prove independence of models and the identity and composition laws.

For a third bounded projective complex $T$ and homogeneous $x,y,z$, both associator routes have quotient coordinate $\bar x\otimes(\bar y\otimes\bar z)$ under step 2. For degrees $r,s$ both symmetry routes have coordinate $(-1)^{rs}\bar y\otimes\bar x$. The left unitor routes send $\bar a\otimes\bar x$ to $\overline{ax}$, and the right unitor routes send $\bar x\otimes\bar a$ to $\overline{ax}$. The coefficient unit sends $1$ to $(1\bmod\pi^j)_j$. In every case the shifted coordinate is zero, preserved by the product cochain maps, so these are equal maps to the fibre, not only equal maps after projection. Localizing gives the asserted coherence diagrams, since the derived associators and unitors are induced from complexes.

For $m\geq n$, the quotient $A_m\to A_n$ sends the $m$-coordinate of the augmentation to its $n$-coordinate: $(x\bmod\pi^m)\otimes(y\bmod\pi^m)$ goes to $(x\bmod\pi^n)\otimes(y\bmod\pi^n)$. Products, associators, signs and multiplication commute with these quotient homomorphisms. In particular all further-quotient squares commute on both coordinates, the shifted coordinate staying zero.

Let $R\to S$ be as in the statement and first use the $\pi$-power quotients $B_j=S/\pi^jS$. The balanced scalar tensorator is $\beta:((P\otimes_RS)\otimes_S(Q\otimes_RS))\xrightarrow{\sim}V\otimes_RS$, $(x\otimes s)\otimes(y\otimes u)\mapsto(x\otimes y)\otimes su$. The same formula in $B_j$ identifies the scalar-extended quotient tensor tower with the quotient tower of $V\otimes_RS$. The finite-free scalar comparison for Roos complexes commutes with augmentations: on first coordinates the two routes send $((x\otimes y)\otimes s)$ to $((\bar x\otimes\bar y)\otimes\bar s)_j$, and both shifted coordinates are zero. Thus the square with $e_{P,Q}\otimes_RS$, $\beta$, and the $\pi$-power completion of the extended complexes commutes. Tensor with $S$ is exact, so it computes derived extension and preserves the quasi-isomorphism. The finite-free strict-tower transport identifies this chain comparison with the canonical derived completion comparison, independently of a chosen basis.

Write $\sigma$ for a uniformizer of $S$. The free $R$-module $S$ has positive rank, since $S$ is a nonzero unital ring; hence multiplication by the nonzero $\pi$ is injective on $S$ and its image in $S$ is nonzero. The DVR factorization gives $\pi=u\sigma^e$. Locality makes $\pi$ a nonunit, so $e\geq1$. Thus $B_j=S/\sigma^{ej}S$. Apply the explicit cofinal Roos restriction $r_e$ to the full $\sigma$-power tower of the extended tensor. It is a quasi-isomorphism and sends its quotient augmentation to the augmentation at levels $ej$. More explicitly its first coordinate is restriction $x\mapsto(x_{ej})_j$ and its shifted coordinate is the block sum of transition images, which sends zero to zero. Together with step 10 this gives the required square in the derived category by inverting $r_e$. It is the comparison through the cofinal quotient maps specified in the statement; no equality of the two indexed towers is assumed.

For $R\to S\to T$, the two scalar tensorator composites send $(x\otimes s)\otimes t$ to $x\otimes(st)$, and for the two tensor factors the scalar is the product of their scalar entries in $T$. Hence their $j$-th quotient coordinates agree by associativity of multiplication. The identity extension sends $x\otimes1$ to $x$. The finite-free product maps have these same coordinate formulas, so their identity and composition diagrams commute. If $\pi=u\sigma^e$ and $\sigma=v\tau^f$ in $T$, then $\pi=(uv^e)\tau^{ef}$; the cofinal restrictions satisfy that two successive cofinal restrictions equal $r_{ef}$, because their first-coordinate restrictions compose and their block sums concatenate the same transitions. The cofinality lemma supplies this composition law. All augmentations in these diagrams retain zero shifted coordinate. Thus the identity and iterated-extension squares, including the cofinal completion comparisons, commute.
